transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Nair, Samir Patel (Redwood) — Dana Lopez, Michael Chen, Rita Gomez, Jonas Eriksson (Orchid)

Summary:
Brief review of Orchid's encryption requirements for ML inference pipeline and the procurement plan for a BYO-HSM (hardware security module) to be used with Redwood Private. Discussed separation of duties, key wrapping, key rotation cadence, audit log export and retention, and legal/escrow conditions. Action items and follow-ups agreed.

Topics covered:
- Encryption at rest and in transit for inference payloads and model artifacts
- BYO-HSM import flow, key wrapping and wrapping key custody
- HSM vendor compatibility, FIPS 140-2/3 and tamper evidence
- RBAC, SSO & delegated admin model for Redwood Console and Private control plane
- Audit logs, TTLs, and SIEM forwarding (splunk/prisma/elk mention)
- Emergency rotation, disaster recovery and subpoena/escrow processes

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Alright hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, I think we have like an hour so we can run through the checklist and then jump into the technical details. Priya is here to cover the HSM/keys flows.
[00:22] Dana Lopez: Thanks Alex. We have procurement kicking off next week so wanted to make sure we understand how Redwood will integrate with our BYO-HSM and what the security boundaries are, especially around key custody and auditability.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Great question. High level — Redwood Private supports BYO-HSM via a key import and key-wrapping model. Customers hold the master wrapping key inside their HSM, and we keep wrapped model keys in our vault. We can do import via PKCS#11 or a wrapped-key exchange.
[00:58] Michael Chen: Quick clarifying Q — are you keeping unwrapped key material ever on Redwood infra? Like plaintext unencrypted keys in memory or disk?
[01:10] Priya Nair: Short answer no for disk. In the runtime we obviously need transient in-memory material to serve models — we use ephemeral key handles that live only in protected process memory and a KMS call pattern to unwrap per-host. The long lived keys are always wrapped with the customer wrapping key. There was a note in our docs — we call our managed KMS the Redwood KMS, sometimes folks see "Redwood Dedicated KMS" in older docs, apologies for the naming drift.
[01:40] Jonas Eriksson: That naming drift actually bit us earlier when we tried to match audit logs. Is there a consistent key identifier that we can map to our SIEM? We need an immutable key ID, rotation stamps, and operation events.
[01:55] Samir Patel: Yes — we emit key operation logs (import, unwrap, rotate, revoke) with a stable key fingerprint which is a 64-bit hex string and the customer-provided key alias, timestamped in UTC. Those logs are part of the audit stream and can be forwarded to your SIEM via our secure webhook or S3 export. Note there might be occasional transcription mismatch in some of our older reports where the service name was Redwood-Infer or Redwood-Serve but the log schema is consistent.
[02:25] Dana Lopez: On audit retention — we need 7 years for certain activities per our sector rules. Is the export immediate or do you provide long-term retention behind your control plane?
[02:38] Alex Chen: We provide both. By default logs are retained 90 days in the console, but we provide automated export to customer-owned S3 or Azure Blob for long term retention; you can set lifecycle policies on your bucket to 7 years. We'll document the exact fields that are exported.
[02:55] Michael Chen: On the HSM side, we care about FIPS 140-2 level 3 or 3+ ideally. Which vendors have you validated with? We saw HashiCorp Vault earlier in vendor list but we need direct HSM vendor compatibility.
[03:12] Priya Nair: We've done integrations with Thales, Gemalto/Entrust, and AWS CloudHSM. On the Vault side that's more software KMS patterns. For BYO-HSM we validated PKCS#11 flows with Thales Luna and Nitro/HSM appliances in customer labs. We'll provide the exact firmware and API compatibility matrix.
[03:35] Rita Gomez: Legal question — during subpoenas or legal holds, can Redwood force-export keys or decrypt data? We need contractual language about access and escrow.
[03:47] Alex Chen: Short answer: Redwood does not have unencrypted access to your master wrapping key. For emergency scenarios we can support a key-escrow arrangement where the customer provides an escrow keyholder or an escrow procedure; this is contractual. We'll put standard contract clauses and an optional escalation flow in the SOW.
[04:10] Dana Lopez: Ok please make that explicit in the SOW — we want no implicit admin access.
[04:18] Jonas Eriksson: Another practical Q — network egress and mTLS between our on-prem HSM gateway and Redwood Private. Is there an option to peer and avoid crossing public internet?
[04:32] Priya Nair: Yes. Redwood Private supports VPC peering, private link equivalents and an on-prem gateway option. For direct HSM connectivity customers typically run a small gateway VM in their VPC that talks to the HSM locally and then opens a mutual TLS session to the Redwood control/data plane with client certs. We recommend mutual TLS plus mTLS pinning and IP allow lists.
[05:00] Michael Chen: Sounds good. What about key rotation — we have a mandated 90-day rotation for some keys, can Redwood automate re-wrapping and rollback safely?
[05:12] Samir Patel: We support scheduled rotations; rotation is basically: generate new data key, wrap with your wrapping key, atomically flip the alias and keep older versions for rollback up to X versions (configurable). There is a short window where both keys are valid for decrypt/serve to allow in-flight requests to finish. We'll show the timing in the runbook.
[05:39] Dana Lopez: We also want separation of duties — our security team manages keys and legal does holds. Can RBAC map to that and integrate with SSO?
[05:48] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Redwood Console supports SSO via SAML/SCIM, role-based access controls and we support scoped roles: Key Admin, Audit Reader, Platform Operator. We can integrate with your IdP and push SCIM groups to map roles. For Private deploys these controls are enforced on the control plane; the runtime enforces policy for key unwrap calls.
[06:10] Jonas Eriksson: How granular are logs for who invoked an unwrap operation? We need user-level or service-account-level attribution plus host identity.
[06:20] Samir Patel: Logs include principal (IdP subject id or service principal), host id, operation, and stack trace on failures. We also include request correlation id to tie back to trace spans in the Redwood tracing system.
[06:38] Michael Chen: One more question: do you support split-key or threshold cryptography? We explored splitting master key among multiple HSMs.
[06:48] Priya Nair: Not out-of-the-box for threshold schemes, but we have customers who implemented a two-HSM handshake where the wrapping key requires two-step approval and separate hardware. We can design an architecture that supports K-of-N with an HSM vendor that supports it, but that will be a custom integration and likely part of the enterprise SOW.
[07:10] Rita Gomez: For the legal hold and escrow, if we provision an escrow holder, what are the controls around who can request a key retrieval?
[07:18] Alex Chen: Retrieval requests require an approved ticket, two-person approval from your side, and an authenticated outward request. Redwood will log and require strong authentication; again, we can put the process in the SOW and include a test drill.
[07:34] Jonas Eriksson: Can we see an example of the audit log schema?
[07:40] Priya Nair: Yes I'll attach a sample JSON schema. It has fields like event_time, operation_type, key_fingerprint, key_alias, actor_subject, host_id, request_id, success boolean, and optional error_code. We'll send a sample to your SIEM integration team.
[07:58] Dana Lopez: Okay let's talk about data in transit — are model payloads encrypted end-to-end if a third party intercepts?
[08:07] Priya Nair: Data in transit between client and Redwood Public API is TLS 1.3. For Redwood Private we support mTLS and optional application-level encryption where payloads are encrypted with a per-request ephemeral key wrapped by your HSM. If you want true E2E such that even Redwood can't see payload plaintext, we'd need an extra encryption layer on the client to do payload encryption and let Redwood serve only deterministic tokens — that's an advanced pattern.
[08:37] Michael Chen: That advanced pattern — what are the tradeoffs? Performance? Cost?
[08:44] Samir Patel: Significant tradeoffs: you lose model-side context if data is opaque, latency goes up due to client-side crypto, and features like embeddings or reranking may not work without plaintext. It's doable for a narrow set of inference tasks but not ideal for general LLM usage.
[09:05] Alex Chen: Quick interjection — for the procurement checklist we will list recommended HSM models, firmware versions, PKCS#11 modules and a simplified network diagram. We'll also flag which items require Redwood support during onboarding vs. customer responsibility.
[09:20] Michael Chen: For service continuity, if your region goes down and we need to failover to another Redwood region, what happens with wrapped keys?
[09:29] Priya Nair: Keys are replicated in wrapped form across regions as per your policy. If you have BYO-HSM we replicate wrapped key blobs only; unwrapping always requires your wrapping key which remains under your control. If you choose multi-region availability we can implement cross-region peering and replication with strict controls.
[09:48] Jonas Eriksson: Any caveats about egress of wrapped-blobs to third-party storage? We want to ensure no plaintext exposure during transit.
[09:56] Samir Patel: All wrapped blobs are transferred over mTLS and additionally can be encrypted with an envelope key. We can also provide an HSM-attested transfer flow using signed manifests.
[10:12] Dana Lopez: On compliance — do you provide SOC 2 Type II reports and ISO27001 certificates for Redwood Private when it's deployed in our VPC?
[10:21] Alex Chen: Yes; Redwood publishes SOC 2 and ISO27001 for our control plane. For Private deployments we have two models: managed Private (Redwood operates control plane in your VPC/region) where we can extend attestations, and fully customer-managed where the customer owns the infra — in the latter case we provide compliance artifacts for the software only. We'll clarify in the contract which model you pick.
[10:45] Rita Gomez: Please add language about evidence sharing cadence during audits.
[10:49] Alex Chen: Will do.
[10:52] [Silence / document sharing for a few minutes]
[16:04] Priya Nair: (screen share) here's the proposed key lifecycle diagram — shows import using PKCS#11, wrapped key stored in Redwood vault, ephemeral unwrapping by runtime, audit log flow to customer S3. Note the small window for in-memory plaintext is minimized and restricted to the inference process.
[16:35] Michael Chen: Looks good. Can you show the logs example again with the field names?
[16:40] Priya Nair: Sure — event_time, op, key_id, key_alias, actor, host, trace_id, success, error, original_request_hash. We'll attach a sample.
[17:02] Dana Lopez: Ok I'm comfortable pending the SOW language and the procurement checklist.
[17:07] Alex Chen: Great. Quick recap of next steps — Alex to send checklist and network diagram, Priya will draft runbook and attach sample logs, Jonas to share network diagrams, Rita to confirm legal hold process. We'll reconvene after you review artifacts.
[17:25] Michael Chen: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[17:30] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up by Monday. Bye.

End of transcript.
